script.speaker: M1

She is too tired to go out tonight.
She feels the same and suggests eating elsewhere.
questions.key_sentence: So am I. Let's try that new noodle place downtown tonight.
questions.key_translation_id: Aku juga. Yuk coba tempat mi baru di pusat kota malam ini.
questions.why_correct_id: **So am I** artinya aku juga bosan. Lalu **Let's try** itu ajakan ke tempat mi baru.
questions.why_correct_en: **So am I** agrees; **Let's try** suggests the noodle place.

questions.analogy_en: A friend who says same and suggests a new spot.
questions.tip_id: **So am I** = aku juga. Cek juga kalimat sesudahnya, sering ada saran.
questions.tip_en: **So am I** = me too. Check what follows.

script.speaker: W1

why_wrong_id.3: Dia tahu esainya penuh coretan, jadi udah lihat.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak rapor yang penuh tinta merah. Tanpa dibaca pun kamu tahu hasilnya.

script.speaker: LEC
script.text: Today we're going to look at an animal that shows how a single species can shape an entire ecosystem: the sea otter. Along the Pacific coast of North America, sea otters live in forests of giant kelp, a seaweed that can grow up to half a meter in a day. Otters eat large numbers of sea urchins, spiny animals that feed on the base of the kelp. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, hunters killed otters for their thick fur, and by the early nineteen hundreds only about two thousand were left. Without otters to control them, urchin populations exploded. They chewed through the kelp, and in many places the forests disappeared, leaving bare rock that scientists call urchin barrens. Fish, crabs, and birds that depended on the kelp lost their habitat. After hunting was banned in 1911, otters slowly returned to some areas, and the kelp grew back with them. Ecologists call an animal like this a keystone species. Just as removing the central stone from an arch makes the whole structure collapse, removing the otter causes the ecosystem around it to fall apart.

script.speaker: LEC
script.text: Visitors to Venice often wonder how a city of stone palaces can stand in the middle of a lagoon. The answer lies beneath the water, in millions of wooden posts. Beginning more than a thousand years ago, builders drove tree trunks, mostly oak and larch, deep into the soft mud until they reached a firmer layer of compacted clay. The posts were packed so closely together that they formed a solid platform. On top of them, workers laid wooden planks and then blocks of a white stone that resists water. Only then did they build the brick walls. You might expect the wood to have rotted long ago, but it hasn't. Because the posts are completely surrounded by mud and water, there is almost no oxygen, and the bacteria and fungi that normally break down wood cannot survive. Over the centuries, minerals from the water have also soaked into the wood, making it even harder. One famous church, for instance, rests on more than one million posts. The real danger today is not rot but rising water, which now regularly reaches the bricks above the stone layer and slowly damages them.

questions.key_translation_id: Karena tiangnya sepenuhnya dikelilingi lumpur dan air, hampir tidak ada oksigen, sehingga bakteri dan jamur yang biasanya merusak kayu tidak bisa hidup.
questions.why_correct_id: Tiangnya terendam lumpur dan air, jadi **there is almost no oxygen**. Bakteri dan jamur perusak kayu nggak bisa hidup.
questions.why_correct_en: **there is almost no oxygen**, so wood-eating organisms can't survive.
questions.analogy_id: Kayak makanan di kemasan vakum. Tanpa udara, nggak gampang busuk.
questions.analogy_en: Like vacuum-packed food: no air, no rot.
questions.tip_id: Dosen bilang **You might expect... but**? Bagian berikutnya biasanya ngejelasin alasan kejutannya.
questions.tip_en: **You might expect... but** sets up the explanation.

questions.prompt: What does the professor say is the main threat to the buildings today?
questions.key_sentence: The real danger today is not rot but rising water, which now regularly reaches the bricks above the stone layer and slowly damages them.
questions.key_translation_id: Bahaya sebenarnya sekarang bukan pembusukan, tapi air yang naik, yang kini sering mencapai bata di atas lapisan batu dan perlahan merusaknya.
questions.why_correct_id: Kalimat terakhir: **The real danger today is not rot but rising water**, yang merusak bata.
questions.why_correct_en: **not rot but rising water**.
questions.analogy_id: Pola **not X but Y** itu kayak papan petunjuk yang nyoret satu jalan dan nunjuk jalan lain.
questions.analogy_en: **not X but Y** crosses out one road and points to another.
questions.tip_id: Di pola **not X but Y**, jawabannya Y.
questions.tip_en: In **not X but Y**, the answer is Y.

script.speaker: LEC
script.text: Let's turn to one of the most puzzling findings in medicine: the placebo effect. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill. Yet in many studies, patients who receive a placebo report real improvements, especially for pain, nausea, and sleep problems. In one well-known experiment, researchers gave patients identical sugar pills but told some that the pills were an expensive new painkiller and others that they were a cheap one. The patients who believed they had the expensive drug reported much greater relief. Expectation seems to play a central role. Brain scans show that when people expect relief, the brain releases its own natural painkillers. What surprised researchers even more was a study from 2010. Patients with a long-term stomach condition were given placebo pills and told honestly that the pills contained no medicine. Even so, many of them felt better than patients who received no treatment at all. Scientists think the ritual of taking a pill regularly may itself trigger the body's response. However, placebos cannot shrink tumors or cure infections, so they are never a substitute for effective treatment.

questions.prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: The causes of long-term stomach problems
Why treatments without medicine can still have effects
questions.key_sentence: Let's turn to one of the most puzzling findings in medicine: the placebo effect.
questions.key_translation_id: Mari beralih ke salah satu temuan paling membingungkan di dunia medis: efek plasebo.
questions.why_correct_id: Topiknya **the placebo effect**: pengobatan tanpa zat aktif yang tetap bisa bikin pasien merasa lebih baik.
questions.why_correct_en: **the placebo effect**: treatments without medicine that still work.

why_wrong_id.0: Obat pereda nyeri cuma dipakai sebagai cerita di eksperimen.
why_wrong_id.1: Masalah perut cuma kondisi pasien di satu penelitian.

why_wrong_en.0: Painkillers are part of a story.

questions.analogy_id: Topik lecture itu payung. Eksperimen-eksperimennya cuma tetesan hujan di bawahnya.
questions.analogy_en: The topic is the umbrella; the experiments are raindrops under it.
questions.tip_id: **Let's turn to** di awal lecture = topik baru dimulai.

questions.prompt: What did the experiment with expensive and cheap pills show?
options: Cheap pills worked faster than expensive ones.
Patients felt more relief when they thought the pill was expensive.
Patients could tell which pills were sugar.
questions.key_sentence: The patients who believed they had the expensive drug reported much greater relief.
questions.key_translation_id: Pasien yang percaya mereka mendapat obat mahal melaporkan rasa lega yang jauh lebih besar.
questions.why_correct_id: Pilnya sama persis, tapi yang dikira mahal bikin **much greater relief**. Jadi keyakinan soal harga ngaruh ke rasa lega.
questions.why_correct_en: Identical pills, but the **expensive** label gave **much greater relief**.

why_wrong_id.3: Pasien nggak tahu itu pil gula.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak air putih di botol mewah yang terasa lebih segar. Botolnya yang bikin beda.
questions.analogy_en: Like water from a fancy bottle tasting fresher.
questions.tip_id: Di eksperimen, cari apa yang sama dan apa yang dibedakan. Hasilnya nunjukin efek dari yang dibedakan.

questions.prompt: What was surprising about the 2010 study?
options: Patients improved even though they knew the pills were fake.
Patients who took no pills felt the best.
The study found no placebo effect.
questions.key_sentence: Patients with a long-term stomach condition were given placebo pills and told honestly that the pills contained no medicine. Even so, many of them felt better than patients who received no treatment at all.
questions.key_translation_id: Pasien dengan gangguan perut jangka panjang diberi pil plasebo dan diberi tahu jujur bahwa pil itu tidak berisi obat. Meski begitu, banyak dari mereka merasa lebih baik daripada pasien yang tidak diobati sama sekali.
questions.why_correct_id: Pasien **told honestly that the pills contained no medicine**, tapi tetap **felt better**. Itu yang bikin peneliti kaget.
questions.why_correct_en: They knew the pills were empty and still **felt better**.

why_wrong_id.2: Kebalikannya. Yang tanpa pengobatan justru kalah.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak trik sulap yang tetap bikin kagum walau kamu udah tahu caranya.
questions.analogy_en: Like a magic trick that amazes you even after you know the secret.
questions.tip_id: Dosen bilang **What surprised researchers**? Pasti jadi soal. Dengerin bagian sesudahnya.

questions.prompt: What warning does the professor give about placebos?
options: They are more dangerous than real drugs.
They work only for sleep problems.
They should be expensive to be effective.
questions.key_sentence: However, placebos cannot shrink tumors or cure infections, so they are never a substitute for effective treatment.
questions.key_translation_id: Namun, plasebo tidak bisa mengecilkan tumor atau menyembuhkan infeksi, jadi plasebo tidak pernah bisa menggantikan pengobatan yang efektif.
questions.why_correct_id: Kalimat terakhir: plasebo **cannot shrink tumors or cure infections**. Jadi nggak bisa nyembuhin penyakit serius.
questions.why_correct_en: Placebos **cannot shrink tumors or cure infections**.

why_wrong_id.2: Masalah tidur cuma salah satu contoh. Ada nyeri dan mual juga.
why_wrong_id.3: Harga cuma bagian dari satu eksperimen, bukan peringatan.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak semangat dari suporter. Bisa bikin pemain lebih kuat, tapi nggak bisa nyembuhin kaki patah.
questions.analogy_en: Like fans cheering: it helps, but can't heal a broken leg.
questions.tip_id: **However** di akhir lecture sering bawa batasan atau peringatan.

items.prompt: Every spring, thousands of cranes ______ through the valley on their way north.
items.why_correct_id: Pelakunya **thousands of cranes**, tapi belum ada verb (kata kerja). Butuh kata kerja lengkap, jamak, kebiasaan: **fly**.
items.why_correct_en: The subject needs a full plural verb: **fly**.

why_wrong_id.1: **to fly** nggak bisa jadi mesin kalimat.
why_wrong_id.3: **which fly** bikin anak kalimat, kalimat utamanya jadi tanpa kata kerja.

why_wrong_en.1: **to fly** can't be the main verb.

items.analogy_id: Kalimat tanpa kata kerja itu kayak motor tanpa mesin. Pasang mesinnya: **fly**.
items.analogy_en: A sentence with no verb is a bike with no engine.
items.tip_id: Belum ada kata kerja di kalimat? Pilih kata kerja lengkap. Aman.
items.tip_en: No verb yet? Pick a full verb.

items.prompt: The new science building ______ by an architect who studied in Japan.
items.why_correct_id: Gedung nggak bisa ngerancang. Gedung dirancang **by an architect**. Jadi pasif: **was designed**.
items.why_correct_en: A building is designed **by** someone: **was designed**.

why_wrong_id.1: **designed** sendirian itu aktif: gedungnya yang ngerancang.

items.analogy_id: **by** itu tanda tangan pembuatnya. Kalau ada pembuatnya, benda itu dibuat: pasif.
items.analogy_en: **by** names the maker, so it's passive.
items.tip_id: Lihat **by + orang** setelah rumpang? Pakai be + V3.

items.prompt: The flight was delayed for three hours ______ the thick fog over the airport.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah rumpang cuma frasa benda **the thick fog**, tanpa kata kerja. Butuh preposition (kata depan) sebab: **because of**.
items.why_correct_en: A noun phrase follows, so a preposition: **because of**.

why_wrong_id.0: **because** itu conjunction (kata sambung), butuh pelaku + kata kerja.
why_wrong_id.1: **so** nunjukin akibat, dan butuh anak kalimat.

why_wrong_en.2: Needs a clause and means contrast.

items.analogy_id: **because of** cukup bawa satu koper, alias kata benda. **because** butuh truk, alias anak kalimat.
items.analogy_en: **because of** carries a noun; **because** carries a clause.
items.tip_id: Cuma kata benda setelah rumpang? **because of**. Ada kata kerja? **because**.

items.prompt: ______ a small café on the top floor of the main library.
items.why_correct_id: Kalimat ini ngenalin sesuatu yang ada: **a small café**, tunggal. Jadi **There is**.

why_wrong_id.2: **There being** bukan kata kerja lengkap, jadi kalimatnya nggak punya kata kerja utama.
why_wrong_id.3: **Being** tanpa pelaku dan kata kerja utama nggak bisa jadi kalimat.

why_wrong_en.3: **Being** leaves no subject or main verb.

items.analogy_id: **There** itu MC yang ngenalin satu tamu. Satu tamu, pakai **is**.
items.analogy_en: One guest: **is**.
items.tip_id: **There is/are**? Lihat kata benda sesudahnya.

items.prompt: The student ______ laptop was stolen reported the theft to campus security.
items.why_correct_id: Laptop itu milik si mahasiswa. Kata penghubung kepemilikan itu **whose**, dan setelahnya langsung kata benda **laptop**.

why_wrong_id.1: **who laptop** nggak bisa. **who** nggak nunjukin kepemilikan.
why_wrong_id.3: **which** buat benda, dan nggak nunjukin kepemilikan di sini.

items.analogy_id: **whose** itu kayak label nama di barang. Laptop siapa? Laptop dia.
items.analogy_en: **whose** is a name tag on an item.
items.tip_id: Rumpang + kata benda + kata kerja? Kemungkinan besar **whose**.

items.prompt: ______ is still a mystery to historians.
options: What caused the city to be abandoned
items.why_correct_id: Rumpangnya jadi pelaku dari **is**. Pelaku berupa anak kalimat harus noun clause (anak kalimat sebagai kata benda): **What caused the city to be abandoned**.
items.why_correct_en: The subject of **is** must be a noun clause: **What caused...**.

why_wrong_id.0: Itu kalimat lengkap. Ditambah **is still** jadi dua kata kerja tanpa sambungan.
why_wrong_id.2: **Why was the city** pakai urutan pertanyaan. Di posisi pelaku harus urutan biasa.
why_wrong_id.3: **Because** bikin anak kalimat keterangan, nggak bisa jadi pelaku.

items.analogy_id: Noun clause itu kayak paket yang dibungkus jadi satu kata benda. Paketnya yang jadi sopir kalimat.
items.analogy_en: A noun clause is a parcel acting as one noun.
items.tip_id: Rumpang di awal, langsung diikuti **is**? Cari opsi dengan **What/Why/How** + urutan biasa.
items.tip_en: Blank before **is**? A noun clause in statement order.

items.prompt: This year's rice harvest was ______ last year's because of the long dry season.
items.why_correct_id: Dua panen dibandingin, jadi comparative (bentuk lebih) + **than**. **small** kata pendek, jadi **smaller than**.

why_wrong_id.1: Polanya **as small as**, dan maknanya sama besar.

items.analogy_id: Kata pendek nempel **-er** kayak stiker. Kata panjang pakai **more** kayak tas.
items.analogy_en: Short words take an **-er** sticker; long ones carry **more**.
items.tip_id: Satu suku kata? Pakai -er. Tiga suku kata atau lebih? Pakai **more**.

items.prompt: Never before ______ so many students apply for the summer research program.
items.why_correct_id: **Never before** di awal kalimat bikin inversi (urutan dibalik). Kata bantu **had** maju: **had the university seen**.
items.why_correct_en: **Never before** triggers inversion: **had the university seen**.
items.analogy_id: Kata negatif di depan itu kayak bel sekolah. Kata bantu langsung lari ke depan barisan.
items.analogy_en: A negative word up front sends the helper to the front.
items.tip_id: **Never, Rarely, Seldom** di awal = kata bantu + pelaku + V3/V1.

items.prompt: Many students try to avoid ______ classes early in the morning.
items.why_correct_id: Kata kerja **avoid** selalu diikuti gerund (kata kerja + ing). Jadi **avoid taking**.

why_wrong_id.2: Dua kata kerja nggak bisa nempel tanpa penghubung.

items.analogy_id: **avoid** itu anggota geng -ing, bareng **enjoy**, **finish**, dan **mind**.
items.analogy_en: **avoid** is in the -ing crew.
items.tip_id: Hafalin geng -ing: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, consider, suggest.

items.prompt: ______ in the forest for three days, the hikers were finally found by a rescue helicopter.
items.why_correct_id: Pelaku utamanya **the hikers**. Mereka tersesat, maknanya pasif. Bentuk pendeknya V3: **Lost**.
items.why_correct_en: The hikers were lost: reduced passive **Lost**.

why_wrong_id.2: **They were lost** bikin dua kalimat lengkap tanpa kata sambung.
why_wrong_id.3: **Having lost them** aktif dan objeknya nggak jelas.

items.analogy_id: Frasa pembuka itu kayak caption foto pendaki. Caption-nya harus cocok sama orang di foto: mereka yang tersesat.
items.analogy_en: The opening phrase captions the hikers: they were lost.
items.tip_id: Frasa pembuka? Tanya: pelaku utama melakukan (-ing) atau mengalami (V3)?
items.tip_en: Does the subject act (-ing) or receive (V3)?

items.prompt: The museum is open not only on weekdays ______ on most public holidays.
items.why_correct_id: Ada **not only**, jadi pasangannya **but also**.
items.analogy_id: Pasangan kata ini kayak gembok dan kuncinya. **not only** cuma kebuka sama **but also**.
items.analogy_en: A lock and its key.
items.tip_id: Lihat **not only**? Langsung cari **but also**.

items.prompt: All participants should ______ their names on the attendance sheet before the workshop.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah modal (kata kerja bantu) **should**, kata kerjanya V1 polos: **sign**.
items.analogy_id: Modal itu colokan satu jenis: cuma muat V1.
items.analogy_en: A modal fits only the base verb.
items.tip_id: Habis **should, must, can**? Langsung V1. Gas.

items.prompt: ______ the students finished their experiment, they cleaned the laboratory carefully.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah rumpang ada anak kalimat lengkap: **the students finished**. Butuh kata sambung waktu: **After**.
items.why_correct_en: A full clause follows; time conjunction **After**.

why_wrong_id.1: **During** kata depan, cuma buat kata benda.
why_wrong_id.2: **Because of** kata depan, juga cuma buat kata benda.

items.analogy_id: Kata sambung waktu itu kayak urutan langkah resep: selesai ini, baru itu.
items.analogy_en: Like recipe steps: finish this, then that.
items.tip_id: **After, before, when** bisa jadi kata sambung. **During** nggak bisa.

items.prompt: There were too ______ people in the lecture hall, so some had to stand at the back.
items.why_correct_id: **people** itu jamak yang bisa dihitung. Jadi **too many**.

why_wrong_id.1: **little** buat yang nggak bisa dihitung, dan maknanya sedikit.

items.analogy_id: Orang itu kayak kelereng, bisa dihitung satu-satu. Pakai **many**.
items.analogy_en: People are marbles: countable.
items.tip_id: Kata benda jamak? **many**. Nggak bisa dihitung? **much**.

items.prompt: By next June, Maria ______ at the university for four years.
items.why_correct_id: **By next June** nunjuk titik di masa depan, plus ada lamanya **for four years**. Jadi future perfect: **will have studied**.

why_wrong_id.0: Present biasa nggak cocok sama titik waktu masa depan.
why_wrong_id.2: **has studied** ngukur sampai sekarang, bukan sampai Juni depan.

items.analogy_id: Kayak argo taksi yang bakal nunjukin empat tahun begitu sampai bulan Juni.
items.analogy_en: Like a meter that will read four years by June.
items.tip_id: **By + waktu masa depan**? Pakai **will have + V3**.

items.prompt: The students in the advanced chemistry class {A}often{/A} {B}works{/B} in the lab {C}until{/C} {D}late{/D} at night.
items.why_correct_id: Pelakunya **The students**, jamak. Frasa **in the advanced chemistry class** cuma keterangan. Jadi **work**, bukan **works**.

why_wrong_id.0: **often** adverb (kata keterangan) frekuensi sebelum kata kerja. Pas.
why_wrong_id.3: **late at night** keterangan waktu yang wajar.

items.analogy_id: Frasa **in the class** itu penumpang. Yang nentuin kata kerja tetap sopirnya: **students**.
items.analogy_en: The phrase is a passenger; **students** drives.
items.tip_id: Coret frasa setelah pelaku, lalu cek kata kerjanya.
items.tip_en: Skip the phrase, check the verb.

items.prompt: The {A}explore{/A} of the deep ocean {B}has revealed{/B} many {C}previously unknown{/C} {D}species{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah **The** dan sebelum **of**, butuh noun (kata benda). **explore** kata kerja. Bentuk bendanya **exploration**.

why_wrong_id.3: **species** bisa tunggal atau jamak. Di sini jamak, pas.

items.analogy_id: Slot setelah **The** itu parkiran khusus kata benda.
items.analogy_en: After **The**: noun-only parking.
items.tip_id: **The ___ of**? Cek akhiran benda: -tion, -ment, -ity.

items.prompt: The volunteers spent the afternoon {A}planting{/A} trees, {B}collecting{/B} trash, and {C}they painted{/C} the old {D}fence{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Daftar kegiatannya pakai -ing: **planting**, **collecting**. Biar sejajar, yang ketiga **painting**, tanpa **they**.
items.analogy_id: Daftar itu kayak barisan baris-berbaris. Semua harus pakai seragam yang sama.
items.analogy_en: A list is a parade in matching uniforms.
items.tip_id: Lihat daftar dengan **and**? Samain bentuk tiap anggotanya.
items.tip_en: Match every item in the list.

items.prompt: The tour guide spoke {A}so{/A} {B}clearly{/B} that even the {C}youngest{/C} visitors understood the history of the fort {D}easy{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Yang diterangin cara pengunjung **understood**, kata kerja. Butuh adverb (kata keterangan): **easily**.
items.analogy_id: Kata kerja itu cara jalan. Yang nerangin cara jalan harus gaya jalan, alias adverb.
items.analogy_en: Describing a verb takes an adverb.
items.tip_id: Kata di ujung kalimat setelah kata kerja + objek? Cek perlu -ly atau nggak.
items.tip_en: A final word after verb + object often needs -ly.

items.prompt: {A}Him{/A} and his brother {B}opened{/B} a small bakery {C}near{/C} the university {D}last{/D} year.
items.why_correct_id: Posisinya pelaku, jadi pronoun (kata ganti) harus bentuk pelaku: **He and his brother**.
items.analogy_id: Coba buang **and his brother**. **Him opened** jelas aneh, kan? Harusnya **He opened**.
items.analogy_en: Drop **and his brother**: **Him opened** sounds wrong.
items.tip_id: Pelaku ganda pakai **and**? Uji satu-satu: **He opened**, bukan **Him opened**.

items.prompt: The researchers {A}have{/A} {B}gather{/B} data from more than {C}two hundred{/C} schools {D}across{/D} the country.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah **have**, kata kerja harus V3. **gather** jadi **gathered**.

why_wrong_id.3: **across the country** kata depan yang pas.

items.analogy_id: **have** itu kernet yang cuma nerima penumpang V3.
items.analogy_en: **have** only lets V3 board.
items.tip_id: **have/has/had** + V1? Itu biang keroknya.

items.prompt: After the conference ended, the delegates {A}returned back{/A} to their hotels, {B}where{/B} dinner {C}was{/C} {D}being served{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: **return** udah artinya kembali. Tambah **back** jadi dobel makna. Cukup **returned**.

why_wrong_id.3: **was being served** pasif continuous yang pas.

items.analogy_id: Kayak bilang naik ke atas atau turun ke bawah. Kata keduanya cuma numpang.
items.analogy_en: Like saying go up upward.
items.tip_id: Hafalin kata dobel: return back, repeat again, advance forward.

items.prompt: Dr. Ramos is {A}a{/A} honest and patient teacher {B}who{/B} {C}always{/C} explains {D}difficult{/D} ideas slowly.
items.why_correct_id: **honest** dibaca dengan **h** bisu: **on-est**. Bunyinya vokal, jadi pakai **an honest**.
items.analogy_id: **a/an** itu dengerin bunyi, bukan lihat huruf. **h** di **honest** diem aja.
items.analogy_en: **a/an** follows sound; the **h** is silent.
items.tip_id: Waspada: an hour, an honest, a university, a European.
items.tip_en: an hour, an honest, a university.

items.prompt: Many residents are {A}opposed{/A} {B}for{/B} the plan {C}to build{/C} a highway {D}through{/D} the park.
items.why_correct_id: **opposed** pasangannya selalu **to**: **opposed to the plan**.

why_wrong_id.2: **the plan to build** pola yang bener.
why_wrong_id.3: **through the park** artinya menembus taman. Pas.

items.analogy_id: Kata tertentu punya pasangan tetap, kayak sendok dan garpu. **opposed** sama **to**.
items.analogy_en: Fixed partners: **opposed to**.
items.tip_id: Hafalin: opposed to, interested in, capable of, responsible for.

items.prompt: The professor gave us {A}several{/A} articles to read and {B}a great deal of{/B} useful {C}feedback{/C} on our {D}researches{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: **research** itu uncountable (nggak bisa dihitung). Nggak boleh ditambah -es. Cukup **our research**.

why_wrong_id.1: **a great deal of** buat yang nggak bisa dihitung, kayak **feedback**. Aman.

items.analogy_id: **research** itu kayak air. Nggak ada dua air, adanya banyak air.
items.analogy_en: **research** is like water: not countable.
items.tip_id: Hafalin uncountable: research, feedback, advice, information, equipment.

items.prompt: Yesterday the committee {A}met{/A}, {B}discussed{/B} the budget, and {C}choose{/C} a new {D}chairperson{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Ada **Yesterday**, dan dua kata kerja lain V2. **choose** harus **chose**.
items.analogy_id: Satu rombongan kata kerja harus dari zaman yang sama.
items.analogy_en: Verbs in one list share a time.
items.tip_id: Hafalin V2 tak beraturan: choose-chose, meet-met, write-wrote.

items.prompt: Only after the storm had passed {A}the rescuers were able{/A} to reach the village {B}that{/B} had been {C}cut off{/C} {D}for{/D} days.
items.why_correct_id: **Only after** di awal kalimat bikin inversi (urutan dibalik). Jadi **were the rescuers able**.
items.why_correct_en: **Only after** needs inversion: **were the rescuers able**.

why_wrong_id.2: **had been cut off** pasif yang bener.

items.analogy_id: **Only after** itu palang pintu. Kata bantu **were** maju duluan buat buka.
items.analogy_en: **Only after** is a gate; **were** steps forward.
items.tip_id: **Only after, Only when, Not until** di awal? Inversi muncul setelah keterangan waktunya selesai.

items.prompt: Each of the new laboratories {A}on{/A} campus {B}are equipped{/B} with {C}modern{/C} {D}safety{/D} systems.
items.why_correct_id: Pelakunya **Each**, tunggal. Jadi **is equipped**.
items.analogy_id: **Each** itu absen satu-satu. Selalu tunggal.
items.analogy_en: **Each** is one at a time.
items.tip_id: **Each of** + jamak tetap pakai kata kerja tunggal.

items.prompt: Of the two proposals, the second one is {A}clearly{/A} {B}the{/B} {C}most practical{/C} {D}choice{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: **Of the two** artinya cuma dua yang dibandingin. Buat dua pakai comparative: **the more practical**.

why_wrong_id.1: **the more ... of the two** memang pakai **the**. Pas.

items.analogy_id: Dua orang lomba itu final: pakai **more**. **most** buat juara umum banyak peserta.
items.analogy_en: Two contestants: **more**.
items.tip_id: **Of the two** = **the more** atau **the -er**. Jebakan klasik.

items.prompt: Students {A}who{/A} wish to {B}join{/B} the photography club {C}must{/C} {D}to register{/D} by Friday.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah modal **must**, langsung V1: **must register**, tanpa **to**.
items.analogy_id: Modal itu langsung gandengan sama V1. **to** nggak diundang.
items.analogy_en: A modal holds hands with the base verb; **to** isn't invited.
items.tip_id: Modal + **to**? Salah. Kecuali **have to**, **ought to**, **need to**.

items.prompt: The book {A}who{/A} I borrowed from the library {B}was{/B} written {C}by{/C} a {D}famous{/D} biologist.
items.why_correct_id: **The book** itu benda. Kata penghubung buat benda **which** atau **that**, bukan **who**.
items.analogy_id: **who** itu kartu nama khusus orang. Buku pakai label **which**.
items.analogy_en: **who** is for people.
items.tip_id: Benda + **who**? Langsung curiga.

items.prompt: When I was a child, my family {A}often{/A} {B}visits{/B} my grandparents in the village {C}during{/C} the school {D}holidays{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: **When I was a child** nunjukin masa lalu. Jadi **visited**, bukan **visits**.
items.analogy_id: **When I was a child** itu mesin waktu. Semua kata kerja ikut mundur ke masa lalu.
items.analogy_en: **When I was a child** is a time machine for the verbs.
items.tip_id: Ada penanda lampau di awal? Cek semua kata kerja udah V2.

items.prompt: The scientists were {A}surprised{/A} by the {B}rapid{/B} {C}grow{/C} of the bacteria in the {D}warm{/D} water.
items.why_correct_id: Setelah kata sifat **rapid** dan sebelum **of**, butuh kata benda. **grow** kata kerja. Bendanya **growth**.

why_wrong_id.1: **rapid** kata sifat buat kata benda. Aman.

items.analogy_id: Kata sifat itu cat. Cat butuh benda buat dicat, bukan kata kerja.
items.analogy_en: An adjective is paint; it needs a noun.
items.tip_id: Kata sifat + ___ + **of**? Hampir pasti butuh kata benda.

items.prompt: {A}Although{/A} the bridge was very {B}old{/B}, it remained {C}in use{/C} {D}despite of{/D} the heavy traffic it carried every day.
items.why_correct_id: **despite** nggak pernah pakai **of**. Yang bener **despite the heavy traffic** atau **in spite of the heavy traffic**.
items.analogy_id: **despite** dan **in spite of** itu kembar beda gaya. Yang satu nggak pakai **of**, yang satu wajib.
items.analogy_en: **despite** and **in spite of** are twins; only one wears **of**.
items.tip_id: **despite of** selalu salah. **in spite of** bener.

items.prompt: The manager {A}suggested to hire{/A} more staff {B}because{/B} the store {C}had become{/C} {D}extremely{/D} busy.
items.why_correct_id: **suggest** diikuti gerund (kata kerja + ing), bukan **to**. Jadi **suggested hiring**.
items.analogy_id: **suggest** itu anggota geng -ing, sama kayak **avoid** dan **enjoy**.
items.analogy_en: **suggest** is in the -ing crew.
items.tip_id: **suggest, recommend, consider** + -ing. Jangan + **to**.

items.prompt: The results of the experiment {A}will{/A} {B}announce{/B} at the international conference {C}next{/C} {D}month{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Hasil eksperimen nggak bisa ngumumin dirinya. Hasil itu diumumkan, jadi pasif: **will be announced**.
items.analogy_id: Hasil itu pengumumannya, bukan penyiarnya. Dia diumumkan, bukan mengumumkan.
items.analogy_en: Results are the news, not the newsreader.
items.tip_id: Pelaku benda mati + kata kerja aksi? Cek perlu **be + V3** atau nggak.
items.tip_en: Lifeless subject + action verb? Try be + V3.

items.prompt: The cat licked {A}its{/A} paws, stretched, and then {B}curled{/B} up {C}in their{/C} favorite {D}spot{/D} by the window.
items.why_correct_id: Rujukannya **The cat**, satu ekor. Kata ganti kepemilikan harus **its**, bukan **their**.
items.analogy_id: Satu kucing, satu pemilik tempat. Kata gantinya ikut tunggal.
items.analogy_en: One cat, one owner of the spot.
items.tip_id: Kata ganti kepemilikan harus cocok jumlahnya sama kata yang dirujuk.

items.prompt: The course teaches students how to {A}write{/A} reports, {B}give{/B} presentations, and {C}leading{/C} {D}meetings{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Daftar setelah **how to** pakai V1: **write**, **give**. Biar sejajar: **lead**.
items.analogy_id: **how to** itu pintu yang cuma muat V1. Semua anggota daftar harus lewat pintu yang sama.
items.analogy_en: **how to** only fits base verbs.
items.tip_id: Lihat kata pertama daftar, lalu samain bentuk yang lain.

items.prompt: There {A}has been{/A} several complaints {B}about{/B} the noise {C}from{/C} the construction {D}site{/D}.
items.why_correct_id: Kata kerja ikut benda setelahnya: **several complaints**, jamak. Jadi **There have been**.
items.analogy_id: **There** cuma penunjuk jalan. Tamunya, **complaints**, yang nentuin kata kerja.
items.analogy_en: The guests after **There** set the verb.
items.tip_id: **There + have/has been**? Lirik kata benda sesudahnya.

items.prompt: {A}Whether{/A} the new policy {B}will reduce{/B} traffic in the city center {C}remain{/C} {D}unclear{/D} to planners.
items.why_correct_id: Pelakunya satu noun clause (anak kalimat sebagai kata benda): **Whether ... city center**. Noun clause dihitung tunggal, jadi **remains**.
items.why_correct_en: A noun clause subject is singular: **remains**.

why_wrong_id.1: **will reduce** kata kerja di dalam noun clause. Aman.

items.analogy_id: Satu paket noun clause dihitung satu barang, walau isinya panjang.
items.analogy_en: A noun clause is one package, however long.
items.tip_id: Kalimat dibuka **Whether/What/That** + anak kalimat? Kata kerja utamanya tunggal.

items.title: Roads of Silk
items.body:
The Silk Road was never a single road. The name, created by a German geographer in 1877, refers to a vast network of routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean for more than 1,500 years. Very few merchants traveled its full length. Instead, goods passed from hand to hand, moving a few hundred kilometers at a time between trading cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar.

Silk was the most famous product carried westward. For centuries, the Chinese guarded the secret of how it was made, and some Roman writers believed that it grew on trees. Wealthy Romans paid such high prices for silk clothing that some officials complained it was draining the empire of gold. In return, China imported horses, glassware, wool, and silver.

The routes were **hazardous**. Caravans of camels crossed deserts where temperatures could fall below freezing at night and rise above 40 degrees during the day, and they climbed mountain passes more than 4,000 meters high. To support travelers, rulers built caravanserais, walled inns placed roughly a day's journey apart, where merchants could rest, feed their animals, and trade.

Perhaps the most lasting cargo, however, could not be weighed or packed. Ideas, religions, and technologies moved along the same routes. Papermaking spread from China to the Islamic world in the eighth century and later to Europe. Musical instruments, recipes, and artistic styles traveled in both directions. Unfortunately, so did disease. Historians believe that the plague that devastated Europe in the fourteenth century reached the continent partly along these trade routes.

The overland routes declined after the fifteenth century, when European sailors found sea routes to Asia that could carry far larger cargoes at lower cost. Yet the term Silk Road has not disappeared. Today it is often used to describe modern projects that link Asia and Europe by railway and pipeline, a sign of how strongly **it** still shapes the way people imagine trade between East and West.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A network of trade routes that carried goods, ideas, and disease
The methods used to produce silk in China
The fall of the Roman Empire
Modern railway projects between Asia and Europe
questions.evidence_quote: The name, created by a German geographer in 1877, refers to a vast network of routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean for more than 1,500 years.
questions.why_correct_id: Teks ngejelasin Jalur Sutra sebagai jaringan rute, lalu barang, bahaya perjalanan, ide dan penyakit, sampai kemundurannya. Jadi isinya jaringan dagang yang bawa barang, ide, dan penyakit.
questions.why_correct_en: The network, its goods, its ideas and disease, and its decline.

why_wrong_id.1: Cara bikin sutra justru dirahasiakan dan nggak dijelasin.
why_wrong_id.3: Proyek modern cuma disebut di akhir.

questions.analogy_id: Main idea itu payung. Harus nutupin semua paragraf, bukan cuma satu.
questions.analogy_en: The umbrella covers every paragraph.
questions.tip_id: Kalimat pembuka yang membantah anggapan, kayak **was never a single road**, sering ngenalin topik.
questions.tip_en: An opening that corrects a belief often states the topic.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, how did most goods travel along the Silk Road?
options: Single merchants carried them the whole way.
They were shipped across the Mediterranean.
They were passed between traders over shorter distances.
They were carried only by Roman soldiers.
questions.evidence_quote: Instead, goods passed from hand to hand, moving a few hundred kilometers at a time between trading cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar.
questions.why_correct_id: Teks bilang **goods passed from hand to hand, moving a few hundred kilometers at a time**. Barangnya pindah tangan jarak demi jarak.
questions.why_correct_en: **goods passed from hand to hand**.

why_wrong_id.0: Kebalikannya. **Very few merchants traveled its full length**.
why_wrong_id.1: Jalur laut baru muncul di paragraf 5.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak lempar bola estafet. Bolanya sampai jauh, tapi tiap pelempar cuma jalan sedikit.
questions.analogy_en: Like a relay: the ball goes far, each runner a short way.
questions.tip_id: Kata **Instead** sering ngenalin fakta yang bener setelah membantah sesuatu.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about the Romans?
options: They refused to trade with China.
Many did not know how silk was produced.
They paid for silk mainly with horses.
questions.evidence_quote: For centuries, the Chinese guarded the secret of how it was made, and some Roman writers believed that it grew on trees.
questions.why_correct_id: Rahasianya dijaga Tiongkok, dan sebagian penulis Romawi kira sutra **grew on trees**. Artinya banyak orang Romawi nggak tahu cara bikin sutra.
questions.why_correct_en: Some believed silk **grew on trees**, so many didn't know.

why_wrong_id.0: Kalau bikin sendiri, mereka nggak bakal bayar mahal.
why_wrong_id.3: Kuda itu barang yang dibeli Tiongkok, bukan alat bayar Romawi. Romawi bayar pakai emas.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak orang yang kira susu cokelat dari sapi cokelat. Mereka nggak tahu prosesnya.
questions.analogy_en: Like believing chocolate milk comes from brown cows.
questions.tip_id: Inference sering datang dari keyakinan yang salah di teks. Keyakinan salah = nggak tahu faktanya.
questions.tip_en: A mistaken belief implies ignorance of the fact.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, which of the following did China import?
questions.evidence_quote: In return, China imported horses, glassware, wool, and silver.
questions.why_correct_id: Teks bilang **China imported horses, glassware, wool, and silver**. Dari opsi, yang ada cuma kuda.
questions.why_correct_en: **China imported horses**.

why_wrong_id.2: Unta dipakai buat karavan, bukan barang impor.

questions.analogy_id: Barter itu dua arah. Sutra keluar, kuda masuk.
questions.analogy_en: Trade runs both ways: silk out, horses in.
questions.tip_id: Hati-hati arah barang: **imported** masuk, **exported** atau **carried westward** keluar.

questions.prompt: The word **hazardous** in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.evidence_quote: Caravans of camels crossed deserts where temperatures could fall below freezing at night and rise above 40 degrees during the day, and they climbed mountain passes more than 4,000 meters high.
questions.why_correct_id: Kalimat sesudahnya nyebut suhu ekstrem dan gunung tinggi. Itu bahaya. **hazardous** = **dangerous**.
questions.why_correct_en: Extreme heat, cold, and height: **dangerous**.

why_wrong_id.1: Umur rute nggak terkait sama contoh di kalimat berikut.

questions.analogy_id: Kalimat sesudah kata sulit itu kayak caption foto. Fotonya: gurun beku dan gunung tinggi.
questions.analogy_en: The next sentence is the caption.
questions.tip_id: Kata sulit di awal paragraf? Baca contoh di kalimat berikutnya.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what were caravanserais?
options: Walled inns where travelers could rest
Markets in the city of Samarkand
questions.evidence_quote: To support travelers, rulers built caravanserais, walled inns placed roughly a day's journey apart, where merchants could rest, feed their animals, and trade.
questions.why_correct_id: Teks langsung kasih definisinya setelah koma: **walled inns placed roughly a day's journey apart**, penginapan berpagar tembok.
questions.why_correct_en: **walled inns** a day apart.

why_wrong_id.2: Celah gunung itu rute, bukan bangunan.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak rest area di jalan tol. Tempat istirahat, makan, dan isi bensin.
questions.analogy_en: Like highway rest stops.
questions.tip_id: Istilah asing sering langsung didefinisikan setelah koma. Baca frasa sesudahnya.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention papermaking in paragraph 4?
options: To explain how merchants kept records of trade
To give an example of a technology that spread along the routes
To show that paper was more valuable than silk
To describe the decline of the overland routes
questions.evidence_quote: Ideas, religions, and technologies moved along the same routes.
questions.why_correct_id: Kalimat sebelumnya bilang **technologies moved along the same routes**. Pembuatan kertas jadi contohnya.
questions.why_correct_en: It illustrates **technologies moved along the same routes**.

why_wrong_id.2: Nilai kertas dan sutra nggak dibandingin.

questions.analogy_id: Contoh itu kayak bukti foto. Kertas jadi foto buat klaim teknologi ikut menyebar.
questions.analogy_en: Paper is the photo proving technology spread.
questions.tip_id: Contoh hampir selalu mendukung kalimat umum tepat sebelumnya.
questions.tip_en: Examples support the general sentence before them.

questions.prompt: The author's mention of the plague suggests that the trade routes
options: were closed during the fourteenth century
questions.evidence_quote: Unfortunately, so did disease.
questions.why_correct_id: Penulis bilang **Unfortunately, so did disease**, lalu nyebut wabah yang menghancurkan Eropa. Artinya jalur dagang juga bawa dampak buruk.
questions.why_correct_en: **Unfortunately, so did disease**: there were harmful effects.

why_wrong_id.3: Jumlah orang dan barang nggak dibandingin.

questions.analogy_id: Jalan yang bawa paket juga bisa bawa debu. Manfaat dan masalah lewat jalur yang sama.
questions.analogy_en: A road that brings parcels also brings dust.
questions.tip_id: Kata **Unfortunately** nunjukin sisi negatif. Itu petunjuk nada penulis.

questions.prompt: The word **it** in paragraph 5 refers to
questions.evidence_quote: Today it is often used to describe modern projects that link Asia and Europe by railway and pipeline, a sign of how strongly it still shapes the way people imagine trade between East and West.
questions.why_correct_id: Kalimat sebelumnya bahas **the term Silk Road** yang belum hilang. Istilah itu yang masih ngebentuk cara orang ngebayangin perdagangan. Jadi **it** = istilah Jalur Sutra.
questions.why_correct_en: **it** = **the term Silk Road**.

why_wrong_id.1: Jalur laut nggak ngebentuk bayangan soal Jalur Sutra.

questions.analogy_id: Kata ganti itu kayak panah. Tarik mundur ke kata benda terdekat yang masuk akal.
questions.analogy_en: A pronoun is an arrow pointing back.
questions.tip_id: Ganti **it** dengan tiap opsi dan baca kalimatnya. Yang masuk akal itu jawabannya.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, why did the overland routes decline?
options: Sea routes could carry more goods at lower cost.
questions.evidence_quote: The overland routes declined after the fifteenth century, when European sailors found sea routes to Asia that could carry far larger cargoes at lower cost.
questions.why_correct_id: Rute darat mundur waktu ada jalur laut yang **could carry far larger cargoes at lower cost**, muat lebih banyak dan lebih murah.
questions.why_correct_en: Sea routes carried **far larger cargoes at lower cost**.

why_wrong_id.0: Wabah nggak disebut sebagai penyebab kemunduran.
why_wrong_id.1: Penginapan karavan nggak dikaitkan sama kemunduran.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak jalan biasa yang sepi begitu tol baru dibuka. Lebih cepat dan lebih hemat.
questions.analogy_en: Like an old road emptying when a faster highway opens.
questions.tip_id: Kata **when** di kalimat sebab-akibat sering nunjukin pemicu perubahan.

items.title: Seeing with Sound
items.body:
On a summer evening, a single bat may catch hundreds of insects in an hour, often in complete darkness. Most bats can see, but in the dark they rely on a different sense. They produce high-pitched calls, usually far above the range of human hearing, and listen for the echoes that bounce back from objects around them. This method, called echolocation, allows them to build a detailed picture of their surroundings using sound alone.

The idea that bats might navigate by hearing was first tested in the 1790s by an Italian scientist, Lazzaro Spallanzani. He found that bats that could not see were still able to fly through rooms strung with wires, but bats whose ears were blocked crashed into obstacles. Spallanzani could not explain this result, because the sounds bats make were impossible to detect at the time. The mystery was not solved until 1938, when an American student used a special microphone to record bat calls for the first time.

Echolocation is remarkably precise. By measuring the time between a call and its echo, a bat can judge how far away an object is. Small changes in the pitch of the echo tell it whether an insect is moving toward it or away from it, and differences between the echoes reaching its left and right ears reveal the insect's direction. Some species can detect a wire thinner than a human hair.

As a bat closes in on its prey, it calls faster and faster, sometimes producing more than 150 calls per second in the final moments. This rapid burst, known as a feeding buzz, gives the bat constantly updated information about the insect's position. To avoid deafening themselves, many bats briefly **contract** muscles in their middle ears with each call, reducing their sensitivity while the call is made and restoring it in time to hear the echo.

Insects have not been passive victims. Some moths can hear bat calls and dive toward the ground when they detect them. Others produce clicking sounds of their own that may confuse the bat or warn it that the moth tastes bad. This long contest between hunter and prey has made echolocation one of the most studied examples of how animals and their enemies evolve together.

questions.prompt: What does the passage mainly discuss?
options: Why bats are active only at night
How bats use sound to find their way and catch prey
The life of the scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
How moths taste to their predators
questions.evidence_quote: This method, called echolocation, allows them to build a detailed picture of their surroundings using sound alone.
questions.why_correct_id: Teks bahas ekolokasi: cara kerjanya, penemuannya, ketepatannya, dan pertahanan mangsanya. Jadi soal kelelawar pakai suara buat navigasi dan berburu.
questions.why_correct_en: Echolocation from start to finish.

why_wrong_id.3: Rasa ngengat cuma detail kecil di akhir.

questions.analogy_id: Main idea itu judul album. Tiap paragraf cuma satu lagu di dalamnya.
questions.analogy_en: The album title, not one track.
questions.tip_id: Istilah yang diperkenalkan di paragraf 1, kayak **echolocation**, sering jadi topik utama.
questions.tip_en: A term defined in paragraph 1 is often the topic.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what do bats listen for?
options: The echoes of their own calls
The sounds made by other bats
questions.evidence_quote: They produce high-pitched calls, usually far above the range of human hearing, and listen for the echoes that bounce back from objects around them.
questions.why_correct_id: Kelelawar **listen for the echoes that bounce back**, gema dari suara mereka sendiri.
questions.why_correct_en: **the echoes that bounce back**.
questions.analogy_id: Kayak teriak di gua terus dengerin pantulannya.
questions.analogy_en: Like shouting in a cave and hearing it return.
questions.tip_id: Scanning kata kerja di soal, kayak **listen for**, di teks.
questions.tip_en: Scan for the verb in the question.

questions.prompt: What did Spallanzani discover in his experiments?
options: Bats with blocked ears crashed into obstacles.
Bats could not fly in rooms with wires.
Bats saw better than humans at night.
Bats made sounds humans could hear.
questions.evidence_quote: He found that bats that could not see were still able to fly through rooms strung with wires, but bats whose ears were blocked crashed into obstacles.
questions.why_correct_id: Kelelawar yang nggak bisa lihat tetap lancar terbang. Tapi **bats whose ears were blocked crashed into obstacles**.
questions.why_correct_en: Bats with blocked ears **crashed into obstacles**.

why_wrong_id.1: Kelelawar yang nggak bisa lihat justru tetap bisa terbang di ruangan berkawat.
why_wrong_id.2: Penglihatan kelelawar nggak dibandingin sama manusia.
why_wrong_id.3: Kebalikannya. Suaranya nggak bisa dideteksi waktu itu.

why_wrong_en.1: Bats that couldn't see still flew through the wires.

questions.analogy_id: Eksperimennya kayak tutup mata dulu, terus tutup telinga. Yang bikin nabrak ternyata telinga ditutup.
questions.analogy_en: Cover the eyes, then the ears. Only blocked ears cause crashes.
questions.tip_id: Kata **but** di kalimat eksperimen sering misahin dua hasil. Cocokkan tiap hasil dengan kelompoknya.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that the microphone used in 1938
options: could record sounds that people cannot hear
was used to block the ears of bats
was too large to use outdoors
questions.evidence_quote: The mystery was not solved until 1938, when an American student used a special microphone to record bat calls for the first time.
questions.why_correct_id: Suara kelelawar biasanya **far above the range of human hearing**. Mikrofon khusus bisa merekamnya, jadi mikrofon itu bisa nangkep suara yang nggak bisa didengar manusia.
questions.why_correct_en: Bat calls are beyond human hearing, yet the microphone recorded them.

why_wrong_id.2: Mikrofon dipakai buat merekam, bukan nutup telinga.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak peluit anjing. Kita nggak dengar, tapi alat khusus bisa nangkep bunyinya.
questions.analogy_en: Like a dog whistle: silent to us, caught by the right device.
questions.tip_id: Gabungkan dua info dari paragraf berbeda: suara di luar pendengaran + berhasil direkam.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, how does a bat judge the distance to an object?
options: By the loudness of its call
By the color of the object
By the time between a call and its echo
By the number of echoes it hears
questions.evidence_quote: By measuring the time between a call and its echo, a bat can judge how far away an object is.
questions.why_correct_id: Teks bilang **By measuring the time between a call and its echo**. Jarak dihitung dari selisih waktu.
questions.why_correct_en: **the time between a call and its echo**.

why_wrong_id.0: Kerasnya suara nggak disebut buat ukur jarak.
why_wrong_id.1: Warna nggak bisa dideteksi pakai suara.

questions.analogy_id: Kayak ngitung jeda antara kilat dan guntur buat nebak jarak petir.
questions.analogy_en: Like counting from lightning to thunder.
questions.tip_id: Soal **how** sering dijawab frasa **By + -ing** di teks.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, echoes give a bat information about all of the following EXCEPT
options: how far away an object is
whether an insect is moving toward it
questions.evidence_quote: Small changes in the pitch of the echo tell it whether an insect is moving toward it or away from it, and differences between the echoes reaching its left and right ears reveal the insect's direction.
questions.why_correct_id: Jarak, arah gerak, dan posisi serangga semuanya disebut. Warna nggak pernah disebut, dan suara nggak bisa ngasih info warna.
questions.why_correct_en: Distance, movement, and direction are listed. Color isn't.

why_wrong_id.0: Ada: **how far away an object is**.
why_wrong_id.1: Ada: **whether an insect is moving toward it**.

questions.analogy_id: Soal EXCEPT itu cari tamu tak diundang. Tiga ada di daftar, satu nggak.
questions.analogy_en: Spot the uninvited guest.

items.title: Reading the Ice
items.body:
Some of the most valuable records of Earth's past climate are not written in books but frozen in ice. In Antarctica and Greenland, snow that falls each year does not melt. Instead, it is buried by later snowfalls and slowly pressed into solid ice. Over hundreds of thousands of years, this process has built ice sheets more than three kilometers thick, with the oldest layers at the bottom.

To study these layers, scientists drill ice cores, cylinders of ice about ten centimeters wide, and bring them to the surface in sections. The work is slow and expensive. A single deep core can take several years to drill, and each section must be kept frozen during its journey to laboratories thousands of kilometers away.

Ice cores are valuable because they contain tiny bubbles of air trapped when the snow was compressed. These bubbles are actual samples of the ancient atmosphere. By measuring the carbon dioxide inside them, researchers have shown that levels of this gas rose and fell with the planet's temperature over the past 800,000 years. Today's carbon dioxide levels are higher than at any point in that record.

The ice itself also holds clues. The ratio of different forms of oxygen in the frozen water reveals the temperature at the time the snow fell. Layers of ash mark major volcanic eruptions, allowing scientists to match events in the ice with historical accounts. Even dust is informative: thick dusty layers indicate periods when the climate was colder and drier and strong winds carried soil from distant deserts.

Ice cores do have **limitations**. Near the bottom of an ice sheet, the weight of the ice above can fold and stretch the layers, making them harder to read. In addition, the oldest continuous record so far extends back about 800,000 years. Several international teams are now drilling at sites in Antarctica where **they** hope to find ice more than 1.5 million years old, which could reveal why Earth's ice ages changed their rhythm about a million years ago.

items.title: Keeping Food Cold
items.body:
For most of history, keeping food fresh was a constant struggle. People dried, salted, smoked, and pickled meat and vegetables, and in cold climates they stored food in cellars dug into the ground. In the nineteenth century, a booming trade developed in natural ice. Workers cut huge blocks from frozen lakes in New England every winter, packed them in sawdust, and shipped them as far as the Caribbean and India.

Ice was soon in daily use. By the 1880s, many city families owned an icebox, a wooden cabinet lined with metal that held a block of ice in its top compartment. An iceman delivered fresh blocks several times a week. Yet natural ice had serious **drawbacks**. A warm winter could ruin the harvest, and ice taken from polluted rivers sometimes carried disease.

Mechanical refrigeration offered a solution. The basic principle, that a liquid absorbs heat as it evaporates, had been understood since the eighteenth century, and inventors built machines that used this effect to make ice. Early refrigerators, however, were large, noisy, and expensive, and many relied on toxic gases that could leak. It was not until the 1930s, when safer chemicals were introduced and prices fell, that electric refrigerators became common in American homes.

The effects reached far beyond the kitchen. Because food could now be stored for days or weeks, families shopped less often and bought larger quantities, which helped supermarkets replace small neighborhood shops. Farmers could send fruit, milk, and meat to distant cities in refrigerated railroad cars, so people in northern cities could eat fresh oranges in winter. Diets became more varied, and illnesses caused by spoiled food became less common.

Refrigeration brought new problems as well. Some of the chemicals that replaced the early toxic gases were later found to damage the ozone layer, which protects Earth from harmful radiation, and **they** were phased out under an international agreement signed in 1987. Today, engineers are working on refrigerators that use less electricity and gases with a smaller effect on the climate, because cooling now accounts for a significant share of the world's energy use.

items.title: Libraries for Everyone
items.body:
Today, most people take it for granted that anyone can walk into a library and borrow a book for free. For most of history, however, books were rare and expensive, and collections belonged to monasteries, universities, and wealthy individuals. A person who wanted to read usually had to buy books or know someone who owned them.

The first step toward public access came with subscription libraries in the eighteenth century. Members paid a yearly fee and could borrow from a shared collection. One of the earliest in North America was founded in Philadelphia in 1731 by Benjamin Franklin and a group of friends who pooled their money to buy books they could not afford individually. These libraries spread quickly, but the fees kept out most working people.

Truly public libraries, paid for by taxes and open to all, appeared in the mid-nineteenth century. Britain passed a law in 1850 allowing towns to fund libraries through local taxes, and the Boston Public Library, which opened in 1854, became a model for other American cities. Supporters argued that libraries would reduce crime, improve workers' skills, and prepare citizens to take part in public life.

The greatest expansion was **financed** by an unlikely source: Andrew Carnegie, a steel manufacturer who was one of the richest men in the world. Between 1883 and 1929, Carnegie paid for the construction of more than 2,500 library buildings in English-speaking countries. He attached one important condition. Each town had to provide the land and promise to pay for books, staff, and maintenance every year, so that the library would not depend on charity forever.

Libraries have continued to change. Many once kept books behind counters, and readers had to ask a librarian to fetch them; open shelves, where people could browse freely, became standard only in the early twentieth century. Today, libraries lend e-books and laptops, offer free internet access, and host classes. For many communities, **they** have become less a storehouse of books than a public space where anyone may learn.
